newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-Global miner's profit slumps with metals prices.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Global miner's profit slumps with metals prices.

text.p: The world's biggest mining company, RTZ-CRA, on Thursday reported a 24 percent slide in annual profit, blaming sharply lower metal prices and problems with a new U.S. copper smelter.
Adverse exchange rates also played a part in the global miner's net profit fall to US$1.096 billion in calendar 1996 from US$1.441 billion in 1995.
The results were in line with industry expectations.
But RTZ-CRA said its prospects remained solid, adding that it saw strong long-term growth in demand for metals and minerals.
It plans capital expenditure of around US$1.5 billion annually over at least the next three or four years and still sees areas that are attractive for exploration and development.

"Whatever the short-term fluctuation in market prices, we believe the group will be a beneficiary of the strong growth in demand for our products which is in prospect over the years ahead," RTZ chairman Robert Wilson said.
Prices for RTZ-CRA's main metals, copper and aluminium, fell 22 and 16 percent, respectively, in 1996.

These are serious concerns for the company as each 10-cent per lb move in the copper price over a year means US$100 million to the bottom line. For aluminium the impact is US$55 million for the same price move.

Adding to the woes of 1996, RTZ-CRA was dogged by delays in reaching peak production at its flagship Kennecott smelter in the United States, which cost US$150 million in lost net earnings, Wilson said.
The smelter was built in 1995 at a cost of US$850 million, but has never operated at full speed.
Wilson said efforts to fix the smelter were under way, including a partial six-week shutdown from April, maintaining that "substantial improvement will become evident during 1997".
More pressing is RTZ-CRA's 67 percent-owned Australian and New Zealand aluminium-making arm, Comalco Ltd.
Comalco recorded a full-year loss this week of A$16.8 million (US$12.9 million), reflecting high operating costs at Comalco smelters and a dismal year for international aluminium demand.
Wilson said Comalco had the unfortunate distinction of being the group's one asset that was unable to operate in the top echelon of the industry production curve.
But he stressed RTZ-CRA was not yet prepared to "cash our chips in" over the aluminium maker.

Bright spots for the miner in 1997 include the first full year of production from the giant Greens Creek mine in Alaska in three years, which is expected to yield 13 million ounces of silver, 55,000 ounces of gold and 36,000 tonnes of zinc.
Copper divisions in Chile and Indonesia are also expected to contribute favourably in the current year.
Later this year, the group will ask shareholders to approve the company's name change to "Rio Tinto", reflecting its beginnings as a Spanish copper miner last century.
The former RTZ Corp Plc was shortened from The Rio Tinto-Zinc Corp in 1987. CRA Ltd was shortened from Conzinc Riotinto of Australia in 1980. RTZ and CRA merged in 1995.
